specialists_or_stages: leader: inventory, component/technology/surface matrix, staffing, deduplication, consolidation (main thread)
ehs-web-api on pulsegate-api (Bun/Elysia HTTP API + nginx edge)
ehs-web-api on tallyflow-consumer (Node Redis-stream ledger/payout worker)
ehs-ai-safety on beaconindex (Python RAG assistant with an LLM tool loop)
ehs-mobile on harborlight-mobile (React Native client API layer)
ehs-web-api with a privacy lens on quarrystore (SQLAlchemy multi-tenant data layer)
ehs-verifier: blind adversarial VER-09 pass over all 53 assertions
architecture.fell_back_and_why: The plugin subagent types (ehs-web-api, ehs-mobile, ehs-infra-cloud, ehs-ai-safety, ehs-verifier) are not registered in this harness, so references/team.md's documented fallback path was used: every role ran as a general-purpose sub-agent with the role file path, its knowledge-pack paths, scope, mode, target language, the full safety contract, the triage rules and the return format copied explicitly into the prompt, since a sub-agent inherits neither the skill nor the leader's context. Dispatched in two waves of at most four in flight: wave 1 (pulsegate-api, tallyflow-consumer, beaconindex, stanchion-ansible), wave 2 (harborlight-mobile, quarrystore), then the blind verifier, which was extended mid-flight to cover quarrystore's assertions once that specialist returned. No specialist failed to return and nothing was dropped for a timeout, so no component is reported from the leader's reading alone. Independently of the specialists, the leader read all 63 files of the tree first, which is what made deduplication and the cross-component chains possible. Audit mode: no file under the target was modified, confirmed by mtime (newest target file predates the run).

ruled_out.assertion: tools.fetch_url is an SSRF sink: the URL is model-controlled and reaches httpx.Client.get, so an injected instruction could request internal metadata endpoints or attacker hosts.
ruled_out.killed_by: beaconindex/beaconindex/tools.py:14-17 — _assert_allowed_host resolves urlparse(url).hostname, lowercases it and requires membership in the two-host allowlist (config/beacon.yaml:48-50); it is called unconditionally as the first statement of fetch_url (tools.py:22) before the client is constructed. Redirect escape is closed by follow_redirects=False (tools.py:24). Credential-prefix bypasses fail because .hostname returns the authority host, and scheme tricks fail because .hostname is None. Residual note: the port is not constrained.

ruled_out.assertion: tools.write_note allows path traversal: name is model-supplied and concatenated into a filesystem path.
ruled_out.killed_by: beaconindex/beaconindex/assistant.py:66-67 — _validate_tool_input enforces the JSON-schema pattern with re.match for every string argument, and the declared pattern for name is ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,63}$ (tools.py:11, referenced at :69). The character class admits neither / nor ., so no traversal token survives, and _run_tool (assistant.py:94-99) is the single dispatcher with no other caller of write_note.

ruled_out.assertion: _verify_producer's BEACON_ALLOW_UNSIGNED environment escape lets an unsigned batch be indexed in production.

ruled_out.assertion: The Qdrant and embedding clients present no credentials and speak plaintext HTTP to a store holding every tenant's documents.
ruled_out.killed_by: beaconindex/config/beacon.yaml:4, 11, 16 — every backend URL is a cluster-internal service address (qdrant.beacon.svc, embeddings.beacon.svc, llm-gateway.beacon.svc), i.e. a private-network binding. ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection through the `order by ${sql.unsafe(orderBy)}` sink, the only non-parameterised query construction in the component.
ruled_out.killed_by: pulsegate-api/src/routes/accounts.ts:25 — resolveOrder() maps the query-string value through the SORT_COLUMNS allowlist and falls back to SORT_COLUMNS.created; both call sites of listMembers (accounts.ts:34 and accounts.ts:115) go through it, so no attacker-authored text reaches the sink.

ruled_out.assertion: POST /hooks/legacy-processor rewrites invoice status with no authentication and no signature verification.

ruled_out.killed_by: pulsegate-api/edge.conf:42 (and 54, 63) — every proxying location sets X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr, overwriting rather than appending, so for traffic through the edge the value is the real peer. The direct-to-port case is not ruled out and is reported as the interface-binding finding.

ruled_out.assertion: Tenant identity is derived from an unanchored regex over the client certificate subject (OU becomes the account id), so a partner could name any tenant.
ruled_out.killed_by: pulsegate-api/edge.conf:32-33 — the certificate must chain to /etc/pulsegate/partners-ca.crt and nginx verifies it when presented, so the DN is issued by that CA rather than chosen by the caller; both maps default to the empty string when no certificate was presented, which makes actorFromHeaders return null (auth.ts:22). ruled_out.killed_by: pulsegate-api/edge.conf — the file declares no proxy_cache, proxy_cache_path or CDN hop anywhere; the only intermediary in the component proxies without storing. Adding Cache-Control: no-store on authenticated responses remains sensible hardening.

findings.title: Retrieval cache key omits the principal, serving one caller the ACL-filtered passages computed for another
findings.class: Cross-tenant data leakage via shared cache (AI-18, CWE-524)
findings.evidence: retrieve.py:13-15 digests only f"{query}\x1f{top_k}"; neither principal.tenant, principal.subject nor principal.groups reaches the digest. _cache is process-global module state (retrieve.py:10). In search() the key is computed at retrieve.py:43 and the hit returned at retrieve.py:45-47 BEFORE group_filter(principal) is ever built, since the filter is only constructed on the miss path at retrieve.py:50. acl.py:24-25 defines Principal.key() returning exactly the tenant:subject string that is missing here.
findings.impact: Within the 120s TTL (config/beacon.yaml:57) any second caller asking the same question with the same top_k receives the first caller's private passages verbatim, across ACL groups and across tenants, since the tenant match at acl.py:49 is on the miss path only. The text is then interpolated into the system prompt (assistant.py:110) and cited back to the wrong user. Common questions collide by construction; no attacker sophistication required.
findings.recommendation: Include the full authorization scope in the key: tenant, subject and sorted groups alongside query and top_k, so a group change invalidates rather than inherits. Change _cache_key's signature to take a Principal so the omission cannot recur silently, and add a regression test that two principals with different groups asking one query get different results.

triage.reason: The only ACL control on this path, group_filter(principal) at retrieve.py:50, sits downstream of the cache-hit return at retrieve.py:45-47 and is unreachable on a hit. may_read (acl.py:55-59) would be the post-filter that saves it; grep over beaconindex/ shows it is never called.
_cache is module-level (retrieve.py:10), shared by every request the worker serves; the crossing principals are the distinct Principal values passed at assistant.py:109.
search() is the single retrieval entry point (only caller assistant.py:109), every call is cached, and no condition narrows caching to a subset of callers or queries.

scope.established_by: Traced _cache through every read and write site (retrieve.py lines 10,19,24,26,31,32,33,43,45,55) and every caller of retrieve.search (assistant.py:109 only).
scope.narrowed_by: Bounded to one worker process and to the 120s TTL at config/beacon.yaml:57. Neither narrows the principals involved, only the window.

searched.for: a principal identity already folded into the cache key elsewhere; Principal.key() looked like the intended scoping helper
searched.found: Principal.key() is defined and returns tenant:subject, but has no callers at all; a helper nobody wired to the cache

searched.looked_in: beaconindex/beaconindex/retrieve.py:36-56 and all callers of retrieve.search
searched.for: a per-request cache reset, a per-tenant cache instance, or a bypass for privileged principals
searched.found: nothing: one module-level OrderedDict, one caller, no bypass parameter and no invalidation hook

searched.for: a deployment artifact showing one process per tenant, which would make the shared dict harmless
searched.found: nothing: no Dockerfile, compose or Helm; CONFIG_PATH is a single hardcoded path and beacon.yaml carries one store.collection shared by all tenants

searched.for: a tenant filter enforced inside the store layer that would apply even to cached values
searched.found: search() takes query_filter as a caller-supplied argument defaulting to None; the engine enforces nothing, so a cached result carries no residual protection

findings.title: search_index tool queries the private collection with raw_search, applying no tenant or ACL filter, and the model can call it
findings.class: Broken access control / retrieval without tenant isolation (AI-14, CWE-863)
findings.evidence: tools.py:39-49 accepts a Principal and never uses it. Line 45 calls store.raw_search(config()["store"]["collection"], vector, top_k), the private beacon_docs collection (config/beacon.yaml:5), through the deliberately unfiltered primitive whose docstring says 'Search with no payload filter. Used by the reindex verifier.' (store.py:74-75); client().search there is called with no query_filter at all (store.py:76-81). The sanctioned path does the opposite at retrieve.py:50. The tool is reachable: declared in TOOL_SPECS (tools.py:74-85), handed to the model unconditionally (assistant.py:87), dispatched via TOOL_REGISTRY (tools.py:91, assistant.py:96-99), results injected back at assistant.py:129.
findings.impact: Any authenticated caller can make the assistant read every document in the shared beacon_docs collection, all tenants and all ACL groups, by asking a question that leads the model to a second lookup. The returned text goes straight into the answer. Full cross-tenant read of the corpus through a normal product feature; also the private-data leg that turns prompt injection into exfiltration. Precondition: one authenticated session.
findings.recommendation: Make search_index call retrieve.search(principal, query, top_k) so it inherits group_filter and the redaction at retrieve.py:52. Give store.search a required query_filter parameter with no default and restrict raw_search to the reindex verifier behind an operator-only module. Wire the already-written may_read (acl.py:55-59) as a post-filter, and add the test that tenant A querying a term unique to tenant B returns empty.

triage.reason: _validate_tool_input (assistant.py:49-74) checks types, lengths, ranges and patterns only and never consults the principal. may_read (acl.py:55) has zero call sites. Qdrant applies nothing: store.py:76-81 passes no filter.
The query originates in the model's tool_use block (assistant.py:127), steered by the user's question and by any injected text in a retrieved passage.
TOOL_SPECS is a module constant with no environment condition and config/beacon.yaml:1 declares env: production.

search_index names the private collection explicitly at tools.py:45 rather than inheriting a scoped one; top_k is capped at 20 (tools.py:82), which limits volume per call, not reach, and the model may call it on each of 6 rounds (config/beacon.yaml:19).

scope.established_by: Compared every retrieval call site in the component: retrieve.py:50 carries the filter; tools.py:45 and retrieve.py:63 do not, and of those only tools.py:45 targets the private collection.
scope.narrowed_by: retrieve.py:63 uses the same unfiltered primitive but targets public_collection, which store.py:45-50 documents as world-readable by design; that call is legitimate.

searched.for: an authorization check in the dispatcher, i.e. whether identity reaches the sensitive operation
searched.found: the principal is passed positionally to the handler but the dispatcher performs only schema validation; no per-tool permission table and no object-level check

searched.for: a post-retrieval may_read filter on search_index results that would make the unfiltered query harmless
searched.found: the function is written and correct, and it is dead: grep returns only its definition

searched.for: a mandatory tenant filter enforced at the store layer regardless of caller
searched.found: nothing: search() defaults query_filter to None and raw_search has no filter parameter, so isolation happens only when the caller remembers to ask

searched.for: per-tenant collections, which would make a collection-wide search self-limiting
searched.found: one shared collection beacon_docs for all tenants; isolation is payload-filter-only, so an unfiltered search reaches everything

findings.title: Guardrails screen only the user's question; retrieved passages and tool results reach the model unscreened and are interpolated into the system prompt
findings.class: Indirect prompt injection / instruction-data boundary (AI-02, CWE-77)
findings.evidence: assistant.py:107 _screen(question, "question") is the only invocation of _screen in the component (definition at :40, this one call). The channels carrying third-party text are never screened: retrieved passages are flattened by retrieve.as_context (retrieve.py:67-73) and interpolated into the SYSTEM prompt at assistant.py:110 via SYSTEM_TEMPLATE.format (template assistant.py:14-24), and every tool result is appended as a user turn at assistant.py:129/140 with no screening. Delimitation is a bare '[{index}] {title}' prefix (retrieve.py:72); a passage may itself contain a line reading '[9] ...' to forge a citation.
findings.impact: An attacker who controls any indexed document, or any page on docs.beacon.internal / status.beacon.internal, writes text the model reads as system instruction. Combined with the unfiltered search_index, injected text directs a cross-tenant read and returns it in the answer or persists it via write_note. The three guardrail regexes (assistant.py:26-32) match three English phrasings and would not stop a paraphrase even if applied here.
findings.recommendation: Move retrieved passages out of the system prompt into a separate data-role turn, spotlight them with a unique per-request delimiter, and state that nothing inside the delimiters is an instruction. Call _screen on retrieve.as_context(passages) before assistant.py:110 and on every tool result before assistant.py:129. Strip bracketed-citation-shaped text from passage bodies so provenance cannot be forged. Treat the regexes as telemetry, not as the control.

triage.reason: _screen is the sole content control and is not on these paths (assistant.py:107 is its only call site); even where it runs it cannot refuse, because config/beacon.yaml:32 sets mode: shadow and assistant.py:45-46 raises only under enforce.

The interpolated value is third-party-writable: as_context renders payload['text'] (retrieve.py:52,72) written by ingest._points (ingest.py:78) from doc.body, which consume_batch accepts from a queue message with no schema validation (ingest.py:123). Tool results come from remote HTTP responses (tools.py:26).
The text lands in the system field of the model request (assistant.py:83), the highest-authority plane, and the model holds live tools (assistant.py:87), so obeyed text becomes tool calls.

scope.established_by: Enumerated every write into messages and system in answer() (assistant.py:110,112,123,129,140) and asked of each whether the text is user-typed or third-party, then checked each against the _screen call sites.
scope.narrowed_by: The assistant message echoed at assistant.py:123 is model output, not third-party input. The user question at assistant.py:112 IS screened; this finding concerns the other channels only.

findings.title: No privilege degradation after untrusted content enters the context: one agent holds private data, untrusted ingestion and an outbound channel with a constant tool list
findings.class: Excessive agency / missing taint tracking (AI-01, AI-06, CWE-269)
findings.evidence: The tool list handed to the model is the unconditional module constant tools.TOOL_SPECS (assistant.py:87), and _run_tool (assistant.py:94-99) resolves from the same constant, so the model's authority never changes after it reads untrusted text. grep for trust_level|tainted|untrusted|provenance across beaconindex/ returns zero matches in any of the seven modules. The three legs coexist: private data via retrieval (assistant.py:109) and the unfiltered tools.py:45; untrusted ingestion via retrieved passages (assistant.py:110) and tool returns appended as a user turn (assistant.py:127-140); an outbound/persistent channel via fetch_url (tools.py:24-26) and write_note (tools.py:35). [VER-09 blind pass, downgraded: VER-09 corrected the scope: the constant tool list and the absence of any privilege degradation after untrusted content enters both HOLD, but 'an outbound channel' does not - fetch_url is host-allowlisted at tools.py:16 with follow_redirects=False at tools.py:24, and write_note writes to local disk, so no tool in TOOL_REGISTRY reaches an attacker-chosen destination. FP-11 applies to the egress leg only. The read-leg harm is carried by the search_index finding, reached through the indirect-injection finding.]
findings.impact: Distinct from the two findings above in what it costs to fix: even with search_index scoped and the context screened, a model that has read attacker-authored text retains full tool authority for the rest of the turn. An attacker landing one document or one line on an allowed documentation host can have the model act with undiminished privilege for up to 6 rounds (config/beacon.yaml:19).
findings.recommendation: Break a leg rather than harden the prompt: mark state tainted once a retrieved passage or tool result enters the context and rebuild the per-turn tool list from that mark, dropping fetch_url and write_note; or adopt a quarantined-model split where the component that reads untrusted text holds no tools.

findings.title: guardrails.mode is 'shadow' in the production configuration, so no guardrail can refuse a turn
findings.class: Security control disabled by configuration (AI-07, CWE-1188)
findings.evidence: config/beacon.yaml:32 sets mode: shadow, and the file's comment at :30-31 documents the semantics ('shadow records what a rule would have blocked without acting on it; enforce refuses the turn'). findings.recommendation: Set mode: enforce for production and keep shadow for a staging profile; since the config path is hardcoded, add an environment-driven profile first. findings.title: gateway.strip_headers omits x-beacon-groups while principal_from_headers derives ACL groups from it
findings.class: Authorization from a client-controlled header / policy-table omission (AI-05, CWE-290)
findings.evidence: config/beacon.yaml:23-27 lists exactly three headers to drop from the inbound request (x-beacon-principal, x-beacon-tenant, x-beacon-request-id) under the comment 'Anything listed here is dropped from the inbound request first.' acl.py:28-39 reads FOUR identity headers: x-beacon-principal (:34), x-beacon-tenant (:35) and x-beacon-groups (:38), the last absent from the strip list. The groups value is split on commas straight into Principal.groups with no allowlist or directory lookup, and that tuple is the entire read-authorization decision (acl.py:50, acl.py:59). The headers establishing who the caller is are stripped; the one establishing what they may read is not.
findings.impact: A caller who can put a header on the request, by reaching the service directly inside the cluster or through a gateway that appends rather than replaces, sets x-beacon-groups to a privileged list; the tenant filter at acl.py:49 keeps them in their own tenant while the group filter stops restricting anything. Intra-tenant privilege escalation to a full read of every restricted document in the tenant.
findings.recommendation: Add x-beacon-groups to gateway.strip_headers; the omission is the defect and the fix is one line. Then remove the dependency on the strip list being complete: resolve groups server-side from subject+tenant, or require a signed assertion that principal_from_headers verifies against a pinned key, so a forged header fails verification rather than depending on a list somebody remembered to update.

triage.reason: Whether the gateway independently overwrites x-beacon-groups is a control outside this repository and no exported artifact, ticket or statement arrived: no gateway config, ingress manifest or mesh policy exists anywhere in the component. Per FP-08 this is UNKNOWN and never HOLDS, and it caps the finding at probable.

acl.py:38 reads the value from the request headers dict and no allowlist constrains it before the filter at acl.py:50; the strip list naming the other three headers is affirmative evidence this one is not cleaned.
group_filter (acl.py:42-52) consumes the header value as truth; may_read (acl.py:55-59) would re-derive the same decision from the same tainted tuple and is dead code.
principal_from_headers is the single construction site for a Principal from a request and its output flows to every retrieval decision; no route builds a principal by another means.

findings.title: _verify_producer accepts any non-empty signature string: the batch producer check is presence-only, not verification
findings.class: Missing cryptographic verification / spoofable origin check (AI-12, CWE-345)
findings.evidence: ingest.py:107-110 returns bool(message.get("signature")) and message.get("producer") in {"crawler","connector"}. There is no key, no HMAC and no digest recomputation: the truthiness of a string is the whole check, and both inspected fields live in the same attacker-supplied message dict, so the message vouches for itself. No signing key or crypto import appears anywhere in the component. consume_batch treats a pass as authorization to index (ingest.py:121-124), and main() feeds it a JSON list from stdin (ingest.py:129,132-133).
findings.impact: Anyone able to place a message on the beacon.documents queue (config/beacon.yaml:39), or run the beacon-ingest console script declared at pyproject.toml:18, is a trusted producer by writing a dummy signature and a known producer name. The docstring at ingest.py:114-117 states the trust assumption explicitly, so the intended control is a signature that was never implemented. Chained with the validation bypass below, the document lands under any tenant and ACL group the attacker names and its body reaches the model's system prompt.
findings.recommendation: Verify a real signature: HMAC-SHA256 or Ed25519 over a canonical serialization of doc plus a message id and timestamp, with a per-producer key from the secret store, compared with hmac.compare_digest, plus a freshness window and replay rejection. Until a key exists, fail closed rather than accept a truthy string.

triage.reason: consume_batch calls index_document directly (ingest.py:124) then store.upsert (store.py:28), which performs no origin check; its docstring only asserts that payloads must carry tenant and acl_groups, which the attacker supplies.
Both inspected fields come from the same untrusted dict the function is meant to judge (ingest.py:110); nothing constrains either to a value outside an attacker's reach.

The test-only escape on the line above (ingest.py:108) is gated on env()=='test' and beacon.yaml:1 sets production, which leaves the presence-only check as the live production behaviour, reachable via pyproject.toml:18.
The claimed control is named in this repository's own code and docstring as something this function performs; it is not delegated to a platform.

findings.title: consume_batch builds Document directly from the queue message, bypassing every DocumentIn validator
findings.class: Validation bypass on a parallel write path / index poisoning (AI-12, CWE-20)
findings.evidence: ingest.py:123 builds the plain dataclass Document(**message["doc"]) (ingest.py:54-61), which validates nothing. The authenticated path does the opposite at ingest.py:92-93 (DocumentIn.model_validate then construct from the validated dump) and the --public path validates the same way at ingest.py:131. Three constraints are enforced on one write path and skipped on the other: the tenant pattern (ingest.py:35), the _reject_wildcards validator on acl_groups with its 1..32 length bound (ingest.py:36-44), and the body size check against max_document_bytes (ingest.py:46-51, config/beacon.yaml:40). Both paths converge on the same index_document -> store.upsert sink writing the shared beacon_docs collection.
findings.impact: A queue message, cheap to produce given the presence-only producer check, writes chunks whose payload carries any tenant and any acl_groups the attacker names (ingest.py:72-73). The attacker therefore chooses which tenant and which ACL group will retrieve the poisoned document, aiming it at a privileged audience; the body then reaches that victim's system prompt via retrieve.py:50 -> assistant.py:110. The unbounded body additionally lets one message expand into unbounded chunks and embedding calls. Stated precisely: a literal '*' in acl_groups does NOT by itself grant broad read, because the filter at acl.py:50 matches the chunk's groups against the principal's groups; the impact is targeted placement, not a wildcard grant.
findings.recommendation: Route the batch path through the same model as ingest.py:93 and :131. Structurally, make Document non-constructible from raw input (accept only a DocumentIn in index_document) so a future third writer cannot repeat the omission. Also handle failure: message["doc"] raises KeyError uncaught inside the loop, so one malformed message aborts the remainder of the batch.

consume_batch is reached from main() at ingest.py:133, and main is the beacon-ingest console script declared at pyproject.toml:18; not behind a debug flag.

findings.title: Producer signature verification runs but cannot fail: signature.mode is 'warn' in the only shipped config
findings.class: Inert security control / insufficient verification of data authenticity (WEB-27, CWE-345)
findings.evidence: signing.js:36 computes matches and :34-35 computes fresh from maxSkewSeconds. signing.js:38-45 is the only decision: on !matches || !fresh it logs a warning and returns false ONLY if config.signature.mode === 'enforce' (line 43); every other path falls through to return true (line 45). config/default.json:21 sets mode: 'warn', and :20 states the intent in-repo ('flip to enforce once every producer ships the signing sidecar'). signing.js:4 also defaults SECRET to '' when TALLYFLOW_SIGNING_SECRET is unset, making matches unconditionally false, which in warn mode is silent. The sole call site, consumer.js:60, branches on the return value, so the branch is dead.
findings.impact: Every event on ledger.events is accepted regardless of signature and regardless of timestamp skew. This is the only origin authentication in the component. Any principal that can XADD to the stream can mint arbitrary ledger.post.v1 postings and payout.release events, i.e. move money to an attacker-chosen destination (handlers/payoutRelease.js:19-28). config/default.json:3 uses redis:// with no username, password or TLS, while Postgres beside it gets ssl.rejectUnauthorized true (:14), so anyone reaching the Redis port is that principal. maxSkewSeconds is computed and equally unenforced, so there is no replay window either.
findings.recommendation: Set signature.mode to enforce and make verifySignature return false on !matches || !fresh unconditionally; treat an empty TALLYFLOW_SIGNING_SECRET as a fatal start-up error. If a migration window is needed, gate the permissive arm on an explicit producer allowlist with a hard expiry, and add a negative test feeding a wrong signature. Give the Redis connection credentials and TLS.

triage.reason: No second verification layer exists in scope. The only other place entry trust is decided is consumer.js:60, which is itself a bypass, not a compensator. No middleware and no second HMAC check anywhere in the ten files.

Boundary named: the Redis stream ledger.events. Producers sign with a shared secret, so the design treats them as a distinct principal; the DLQ tool is a third.

findings.title: entry.verified is an unauthenticated in-band trust marker that skips signature verification; DLQ replay launders bad-signature entries into it
findings.class: Authentication bypass / reliance on untrusted input in a security decision (CWE-807)
findings.evidence: consumer.js:60: if (entry.verified !== '1' && !verifySignature(...)). entry is built by fieldsToObject (consumer.js:41-45) directly from the raw Redis stream field list the producer supplies to XADD. The && short-circuits, so when verified === '1' verifySignature is never called. Two writers: (1) dlq.js:37 xadd(stream,'*','body',entry.body,'verified','1') inside replay(), which reads the DLQ with xrange('-','+') (dlq.js:32) and loops over EVERY entry with no filter on entry.reason, while consumer.js:62 parks entries with reason 'bad-signature' on that exact stream; replay also drops the signature field so a replayed entry could not be re-verified. (2) Any producer with XADD can set the field on the first write; nothing distinguishes it from one written by dlq.js.
findings.impact: Any event can be made to skip signature verification permanently: an attacker sets verified=1 on their own XADD, or gets one poisoned message parked (trivial, since any malformed envelope or bad signature parks it) and waits for the routine operator action npm run dlq replay, which re-injects it as trusted. The second route is a confused deputy, since the DLQ tool's own comment (dlq.js:27-30) tells the operator the entries were checked on the way in, which is false for the bad-signature reason. This is the bypass that outlives fixing signature.mode, so the two must be fixed together.
findings.recommendation: Never carry a verification verdict in-band on the channel the untrusted producer writes. Delete the entry.verified short-circuit and verify every entry unconditionally. For replay, re-add the original signature field so the consumer re-verifies, and refuse to replay entries whose reason is bad-signature.

findings.title: The payout path writes balances through adjustBalance, which enforces neither the solvency check nor the per-entry ceiling its sibling applyPosting enforces

findings.title: Idempotency claim is never released on failure and its key is producer-chosen: a payout is silently dropped and acknowledged
findings.class: Business logic / a declared recovery control with zero callers (WEB-17, CWE-754)
findings.evidence: payoutRelease.js:12 claims the key before doing any work; idempotency.js:16 writes {state:'in-flight'} with EX 604800 (7 days). If anything after the claim throws (the payouts insert at :19 or the balance write at :28) the key stays in-flight for a week. makeIdempotency exports a release function for exactly this (idempotency.js:27-29) and it has ZERO callers; grep for 'release(' returns only its own definition and pg's unrelated client.release() at ledger.js:46. On the next delivery claim.fresh is false and the handler returns claim.previous?.result ?? {status:'in-flight'} (:15), a NORMAL return, so consumer.js:98-99 XACKs the entry. The log line says 'payout already released, replaying result', the opposite of what happened. The key is chosen by the message (payoutRelease.js:10) and namespaced only by the global 'ik:' prefix (idempotency.js:15).
findings.impact: One transient database error permanently loses a payout while the system records success, and the 7-day TTL means the loss is not self-healing. Separately, because idempotencyKey is attacker-supplied with no namespace, anyone who can place an event and predict another producer's key (an order id, an invoice reference) can pre-claim it, after which the legitimate payout is answered with in-flight and acked without executing. There is also no reclaim path: the loop reads only '>' (consumer.js:91) and no xautoclaim/xpending exists, so an entry whose handler threw is caught and swallowed at :100-102 and never acked.
findings.recommendation: Call idempotency.release(key) in a catch/finally so a failed attempt frees its claim, and stop returning a success-shaped value for the in-flight state, throwing instead so consumer.js does not XACK. Distinguish done from in-flight at the call site. Namespace the key by account and producer so one producer cannot squat another's, and add an XAUTOCLAIM-based reclaim.

The key is traced to the message at payoutRelease.js:10; on v1 the schema bounds it only by maxLength 128 with no format or namespace, and on v2 it is unbounded.

findings.title: Bastion auth logs are forwarded in cleartext TCP to the syslog-over-TLS port

findings.evidence: roles/bastion/tasks/main.yml:34-39 writes /etc/rsyslog.d/50-bastion.conf containing 'auth,authpriv.*  @@logs.stanchion.net:6514'. Neither appears in the copied content, and no other rsyslog configuration exists in the component. Port 6514 is the IANA-registered syslog-over-TLS port, so the target expects TLS while the sender as configured does not negotiate it.

Sent unencrypted they are readable and modifiable by anyone positioned between jump-01 and the collector, which also means the audit trail for the fleet's only SSH entry point is tamperable in transit. Secondary effect: if the collector enforces TLS on 6514, the forwarder silently fails and the bastion's auth logs are not collected at all.
findings.recommendation: Configure the TLS driver explicitly in the same file: set $DefaultNetstreamDriver gtls, $DefaultNetstreamDriverCAFile to the collector's CA, $ActionSendStreamDriverMode 1 and $ActionSendStreamDriverAuthMode x509/name before the forwarding rule, and manage the CA file with the same role. Verify the negotiated session on the collector rather than assuming the port implies the protocol.

auth/authpriv is the authentication audit trail of the fleet's jump host, so the data has security value by definition.

findings.title: The WebView bridge hands the live access token to whatever document is loaded, and the pane accepts any origin
findings.class: Exposed dangerous method to untrusted content / token exfiltration (MOB-06, CWE-749)
findings.evidence: WebPane.tsx:52 injects BRIDGE with injectedJavaScriptBeforeContentLoaded, so window.harborlight.requestToken() (:14-22) exists in every document the pane loads, before that document's own scripts run. WebPane.tsx:49 sets originWhitelist={['*']}, with javaScriptEnabled and domStorageEnabled on (:50-51). On receiving {kind:'token'} the handler at :32-34 injects window.harborlight.onToken(<access token>) back into the page with no check of what page asked. There is no onShouldStartLoadWithRequest and no onNavigationStateChange in the file, so a first-party page that redirects, or an iframe-driven top-level navigation, keeps the bridge on the new origin.
findings.impact: Any document reachable in this pane obtains the account bearer token with a single JS call and exfiltrates it to an attacker-controlled host. Combined with the unvalidated deep-link URL, the precondition is only that the victim taps a link: harborlight://web?url=https://attacker.example/ loads the attacker's page, which calls requestToken() and posts the token out. With the token the attacker drives the API as the user, including createTransfer/confirmTransfer, which require no step-up. Second principal: the operator of any origin loaded in the pane, including a compromised third-party script on the legitimate web surface. No device access and no network position needed.

Better still, stop shipping the token to page JS at all: have the web surface authenticate with its own short-lived, audience-scoped, single-use ticket minted server-side.

The uri prop is attacker-influenceable: the only producer in scope is nav.openWebPane(...) at router.ts:55, whose URL comes straight from the deep-link query string.
The construct is exactly as wide as it reads: ['*'] at WebPane.tsx:49 with no per-navigation condition anywhere in the file to narrow it.

findings.title: The biometric step-up returns true without prompting for 120 seconds, and the function that would reset the window is never called
findings.class: Local authentication not bound to a key, with an unbounded validity window (MOB-16, CWE-603)
findings.evidence: biometric.ts:19 short-circuits with 'if (Date.now() - lastPromptAt < STEP_UP_WINDOW_MS) return true' — no OS prompt, no keychain access, nothing cryptographic. STEP_UP_WINDOW_MS is 120000 (:6). forgetPresence() (:37-38) is the only thing that would invalidate the window, and a grep returns its definition and nothing else, so the window is not cleared on logout (session.ts:40-45 does not touch it), on backgrounding (no AppState listener exists in the component), or on session change. Even on the prompting path the result is a boolean branch: the keychain entry read at :21-24 is discarded, so nothing is unwrapped or decrypted by the success.
findings.impact: Whoever holds the unlocked phone within two minutes of any legitimate confirmation performs every step-up-gated action with no prompt: changeEmail, updateProfile, freezeCard. Email change is the account-recovery pivot, so this converts two minutes of physical access into an account takeover path. Because forgetPresence is dead, the window also survives a logout/login cycle within the same process. Not assertable from source: whether the backend independently requires strong customer authentication on these operations.
findings.recommendation: Either remove the window entirely for money-moving and account-recovery actions, or cut it to roughly 30 seconds and make it bounded: call forgetPresence() from session.clear(), from an AppState listener on background, and after any step-up-gated call completes. More fundamentally, bind the step-up to a key instead of a boolean: have the success unwrap a Keychain/Keystore item created with BIOMETRY_CURRENT_SET (the enrol path at biometric.ts:31-34 already creates a suitable item) and use the unwrapped material to sign the request, so there is no branch to flip and no window to ride. Enforce the step-up server-side regardless.

triage.reason: Whether the server independently re-authorizes these actions cannot be established: the backend is not in scope and no artifact stating an authentication policy is present. Reported as probable on the client-side evidence; the UNKNOWN is what caps the status.
The actions behind the gate are not read-only: changeEmail (account recovery), freezeCard and updateProfile at endpoints.ts:11,13,10.
It does not reduce to informational: an unbound check is a defect under any profile and must be reported with the adversary declared, not silently dropped.

findings.class: Insecure default that fails open on a security-relevant configuration (MOB-10, CWE-1188)

findings.title: Migration 0007 inserts a demo firm and a demo principal into every database it upgrades
findings.class: Test data in a production migration (CWE-1188)
findings.evidence: Read key by key: lines 19-23 add category, billable_minutes and redacted_at, matching models.py:64-66; lines 24-25 create the case_id and firm_id indexes; lines 29-36 insert firms('firm_demo', 'Demo & Partners'); lines 37-45 insert principals('prn_demo', 'firm_demo', 'clerk@example.invalid', 'standard', false). The comment at lines 27-28 asserts the demo firm 'is skipped by every production query filter'; a package-wide grep for firm_demo and prn_demo returns only these three lines, and no filter in models.py, session.py, policy.py, repository.py, search.py or exports.py excludes it, while session.py:46-49 would narrow queries TO that firm rather than away from it. downgrade (lines 48-53) drops the columns and indexes and leaves both rows behind.
findings.impact: A standing principal row in the production database is an identity the whole component trusts: policy.can_read/can_write (policy.py:37-53) authorize whatever that row's firm and clearance say, and the firm exists, so its rows pass the scoping guard normally. Whoever can authenticate as clerk@example.invalid, or whose identity provider maps to that email (models.py:36 makes email unique, so it is the natural join key), acts as a valid principal.
findings.recommendation: Move the seed into the test fixture that needs it, add a data migration deleting the two rows created by 0007 where they still exist, make downgrade symmetric, and add a CI check that fails a migration containing an INSERT into firms or principals.

triage.reason: This is the shipped alembic revision (revision = '0007_case_notes', line 12) and the inserts sit in upgrade() with no environment check around them, so they run wherever the migration runs.
A principals row is an identity with a firm and a clearance, not inert sample content; the email domain is reserved (.invalid) but the row's authority is real.

The migration's own comment claims a production query filter skips the demo firm. No such filter exists in the nine files in scope, but the authentication and API layers were not in scope and no artifact from them arrived, so per FP-08 this is UNKNOWN and the finding is capped at probable.

scope.established_by: Key-by-key reading of the migration followed by a package-wide grep for the seeded identifiers.
scope.narrowed_by: The seeded principal has clearance 'standard' (rank 20) and is_staff false, so it does not by itself reach sealed matters; and 'on conflict do nothing' means a second run does not overwrite an existing row.

searched.for: the production query filter the comment claims skips the demo firm
searched.found: only the three lines inside the migration itself; no filter exists in any of the nine source files

searched.for: a scoping rule that would exclude a demo tenant from ordinary queries
searched.found: the listener narrows queries to the current firm, which includes firm_demo when that is the current firm; it excludes nothing

searched.for: removal of the seeded rows on rollback
searched.found: only the columns and indexes are dropped; both inserted rows survive a downgrade

searched.for: a test configuration that would run this seed only under pytest
searched.found: testpaths = ["tests"], so the fixture path is separate from the migration and the seed is not a test-only artifact

findings.title: Exported CSVs embed note bodies unescaped, so a note beginning with = is a formula in the spreadsheet that opens it
findings.class: CSV formula injection (CWE-1236)
findings.evidence: All three writers put stored text straight into a cell: exports.py:30-32 (note body), exports.py:65-67 (note body, bundle) and exports.py:44-47 (docket summary). csv.QUOTE_ALL (exports.py:27, 42, 62) is CSV-level quoting and does not stop a spreadsheet from evaluating a leading =, +, -, @, tab or carriage return once the field is unquoted. The only validation the body ever receives is repository._validate_body (repository.py:35-40), which rejects an empty body and one over MAX_BODY_CHARS and constrains no characters; create_note passes the body straight through at repository.py:57 and update_note at :76.
findings.impact: The case-team member who opens the export, or the court reporting feed that ingests the nightly docket dump (exports.py:37), executes the formula with their own privileges: HYPERLINK- or WEBSERVICE-style payloads exfiltrate neighbouring cells of privileged matter content to an external host. Preconditions: the attacker authors a note and a different person later opens the CSV; modern spreadsheet defaults prompt before external calls, which is why this is rated low.
findings.recommendation: Add one escaping helper used by all three writers that prefixes any cell whose first character is =, +, -, @, tab or CR with a single quote, and prefer a typed format such as XLSX or JSON for exports of free text.

triage.reason: Note bodies are free text written by principals (repository.py:57, 76) and the only filter on them, _validate_body, checks emptiness and length only.

The sink is not inert text: the file is a CSV whose declared consumer is a spreadsheet the case team downloads (exports.py:22) and a reporting feed (exports.py:37), and QUOTE_ALL does not disable formula evaluation.
Author and reader are different principals, and for write_docket_csv the reader is outside the firm entirely.
It is not merely informational, since code executes in the victim's spreadsheet, but the modern-client prompt bounds it, which is reflected in the low severity rather than by closing the finding.

scope.established_by: Enumerated every csv.writer call in the component and traced each written column back to its origin in models.py.
scope.narrowed_by: The docket writer (exports.py:44-47) emits only material already cleared for publication (models.py:73-78), so a payload there must first pass a releasing partner; the two note writers have no such step.

searched.for: an escaping or sanitising step before the value reaches the cell
searched.found: only csv.QUOTE_ALL, which is quoting rather than neutralisation; no prefix guard and no helper

searched.for: input validation that would reject a leading formula character
searched.found: an emptiness check and a 20,000-character cap; no character constraints

searched.for: a spreadsheet or sanitisation library whose writer would escape formulas automatically
searched.found: no such dependency; the standard-library csv module is used directly

findings.title: The exfiltration-url guardrail is bypassed by putting the internal marker anywhere in the URL, so the rule is useless even once enforcement is switched on
findings.class: Ineffective security control / unbounded negative lookahead (CWE-625)
findings.evidence: assistant.py:31 is re.compile(r"https?://(?!\S*\.beacon\.internal)\S+/[a-z0-9]{16,}", re.I). The negative lookahead is anchored immediately after the scheme, but its inner \S* is unbounded, so it scans the entire non-whitespace run rather than just the host. Any occurrence of '.beacon.internal' later in the URL therefore satisfies the lookahead and suppresses the match. Executed against the compiled pattern: 'https://evil.example/aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa' matches (rule fires), while 'https://evil.example/aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa?x=.beacon.internal' and the same URL with '#.beacon.internal' both fail to match, so the rule stays silent on an exfiltration URL pointed at an attacker host. This finding was raised by the independent blind VER-09 pass, which had these files open and noticed a defect no specialist asserted; the bypass above was then reproduced directly against the pattern.
findings.impact: The rule intended to catch data leaving for a non-internal host does not survive a suffix an attacker fully controls. It matters because it is not currently load-bearing for the reason one would hope: the mode is 'shadow', so nothing fires today. The consequence is that fixing guardrails.mode to 'enforce' would produce a system that looks defended and is not, and the two defects therefore have to be fixed together or the remediation reads as complete when it is not.
findings.recommendation: Bound the lookahead to the authority component rather than the whole URL: parse the URL and compare the host against the internal-domain allowlist, exactly as tools._assert_allowed_host already does at tools.py:14-17, instead of matching a marker anywhere in the string. Treat the regex family as telemetry, and rely on the host allowlist for the actual control.

triage.reason: No other control catches an exfiltration URL in model output: _screen (assistant.py:40-46) is the only content check, and this is one of its three rules.
The bypass string is fully attacker-authored: the URL appears in text the model emits or in a retrieved passage, both third-party writable.

Bounded to medium rather than higher: because guardrails.mode is 'shadow' (config/beacon.yaml:32) the rule cannot refuse a turn today either way, so this defect has no independent impact until that flag is flipped. It downgrades the severity; the finding stays written down precisely because the flag fix would otherwise look sufficient.

scope.established_by: Compiled the exact pattern from source and executed it against a matching and a bypassing URL, then traced the rule to its only consumer (_guardrail_hits at assistant.py:37, called from _screen at :41).
scope.narrowed_by: config/beacon.yaml:32 keeps the whole rule set inert today, so this is latent rather than active; the other two rules in the dict are not affected by this defect.

searched.for: whether the other two guardrail rules share the same unbounded-lookahead defect, which would widen the finding
searched.found: they do not: untrusted-instruction and credential-shape are plain alternations with no lookahead, so the defect is specific to exfiltration-url

searched.for: whether a correct host check already exists elsewhere in the component that this rule could reuse
searched.found: _assert_allowed_host parses with urlparse and compares .hostname against a config allowlist, which is the correct shape and is what the recommendation points at

searched.for: a second consumer of the pattern, or a post-match verification that would catch the miss
searched.found: nothing: _guardrail_hits returns rule names by search() alone, and _screen acts only on a non-empty list

findings.title: attachSessionToken places the live access token in a URL query parameter that the WebView then loads
findings.class: Credential in a URL query string (CWE-598)
findings.evidence: session.ts:55-61: after confirming url.origin === PROFILE.webOrigin (:59), the function does url.searchParams.set('sso', token) at :60 and returns the serialised URL, which router.ts:55 hands to nav.openWebPane as the address the pane loads. The token is the same live bearer returned by currentAccessToken() (session.ts:47-49) and used for API calls at client.ts:26. This finding was raised by the independent blind VER-09 pass, which noted that the origin check at :59 addresses who receives the token and not the channel it travels in.
findings.impact: A credential in a query string is written to places a header is not: the web server's access logs, the Referer header of any outbound link the loaded page contains, browser and WebView history, and any analytics or error reporter on that page that captures the current URL. The origin check does bound the recipient to the first-party web surface, so this is not a handoff to an attacker's host; it is a durable disclosure of a live session token into logs and third-party referers that survives the session in which it was issued.
findings.recommendation: Do not put the bearer in the URL. Mint a short-lived, single-use, audience-scoped exchange ticket server-side and put that in the query, or hand the token to the page over the existing postMessage bridge after the origin has been verified. If the parameter must stay for now, make it one-time-use server-side and strip it from the address bar on load.

triage.reason: The origin comparison at session.ts:59 is the only control, and it constrains the destination rather than the channel; nothing removes the parameter after load or limits its lifetime.
This is a disclosure of a value the app itself holds, not the injection of an attacker-controlled one.
The value is a live session bearer token, the credential the whole API surface trusts.
The narrowing at :59 is real and is stated in the impact, but within the first-party origin the token still lands in the URL on every web-pane open.

scope.established_by: Read attachSessionToken end to end and followed its single caller into the pane, confirming the returned string is used as the WebView address.
scope.narrowed_by: session.ts:59 restricts the parameter to PROFILE.webOrigin, so a foreign origin never receives it; that is what separates this finding from the deep-link and bridge findings.

searched.for: the pane stripping the sso parameter after load, or loading it by POST instead of as a URL
searched.found: nothing: source={{ uri }} loads the URL as given, and no navigation handler rewrites it

searched.looked_in: harborlight-mobile/src/ grep for attachSessionToken and sso
searched.for: another consumer that might exchange the parameter for a cookie and discard it
searched.found: two hits only, the definition at session.ts:55 and the call at router.ts:55; no exchange step exists in the component

searched.for: an expiry on the token that would bound how long a leaked URL stays useful
searched.found: the Tokens type carries expiresAt, but restore() sets it to 0 at :36 and no code path in the component checks it, so lifetime is not enforced client-side

findings.title: The app attaches its own bearer token to the backend-supplied upload URL on the ordinary upload path, not only the deep-link one
findings.class: Credential sent to a host outside the API origin (CWE-200)
findings.evidence: putBytes (uploads.ts:31-43) sets authorization: `Bearer ${currentAccessToken() ?? ''}` at :39 on a request to targetUrl, an absolute URL the function receives rather than one derived from PROFILE.apiBase. On the normal path that URL is whatever the backend returned in the ticket at uploads.ts:58-61 and is passed through at :74. The request uses the global fetch at :33, so it also bypasses the pinned transport used by call(). This finding was raised by the independent blind VER-09 pass; the deep-link finding covers only the attacker-chosen destination, and this is the same header on the everyday path.
findings.impact: If the storage URL points at a third-party object store, which is the usual reason a backend hands back a separate upload target at all, the app's own session bearer is disclosed to that host and to its access logs on every document upload. The credential is not needed there: a presigned URL carries its own authorisation in the query string. Precondition and the reason this is probable rather than confirmed: whether targetUrl is first-party or third-party is decided by the backend, which is not in this tree.
findings.recommendation: Attach the Authorization header only when the request target is the app's own API origin; for a storage target send no bearer and rely on the presigned URL. Route the upload through the pinned transport, or pin the storage host explicitly, so the bytes and any credential are not exposed to an unpinned TLS session.

triage.reason: No control limits which hosts receive the header: putBytes takes an absolute URL and sets the header unconditionally, with no origin comparison anywhere in the file.

If the backend always returns a first-party storage URL under the same trust boundary, the exposure would be intended and bounded. Nothing in this tree establishes what host the ticket contains; per FP-08's doctrine that absence of evidence is never HOLDS, this caps the finding at probable. What would settle it: one example ticket response, or the backend's storage configuration.
The disclosed value is the live session bearer.
Both callers of putBytes reach the same header: createUpload at uploads.ts:74 and resumeUpload at :96, so the construct is not narrower than it reads.

scope.established_by: Read putBytes and enumerated both of its call sites, then traced targetUrl back to the ticket returned by the API at uploads.ts:58-61.
scope.narrowed_by: On the ordinary path the URL comes from the authenticated backend rather than from an attacker, which is exactly what separates this from the deep-link resume finding; the header is identical on both.

searched.for: an origin check or a conditional that would omit the Authorization header for a non-API host
searched.found: nothing: the header block is unconditional and the function never inspects targetUrl

searched.for: a declared storage origin that would let the app distinguish first-party storage from a third party
searched.found: the Profile type carries apiBase, fallbackBase, certificatePins and webOrigin only; no storage origin exists to compare against

searched.for: whether the component's own convention is to send the bearer only through the pinned transport
searched.found: it is: send() attaches headers() including the bearer and always passes an sslPinning option, so putBytes's use of the global fetch is the outlier

findings.title: The sensitivity axis fails open in the same way the clearance axis does: an unrecognised case sensitivity is treated as 'standard'
findings.class: Fail-open authorization on the second policy axis (CWE-1188)
findings.evidence: policy.py:40 and policy.py:53 both compare against SENSITIVITY_RANK.get(case.sensitivity, 20). The table (policy.py:20-25) defines public/standard/privileged/sealed, and the fallback 20 equals 'standard', so a case whose sensitivity is not one of the four literals is treated as an ordinary matter. models.py:50 declares sensitivity as a plain String(32) with default 'standard' and no constraint; a package-wide search for CheckConstraint, Enum and validates returns nothing, and migration 0007 adds no constraint. This finding was raised by the independent blind VER-09 pass, which observed that the clearance-side fallback was asserted and its mirror image on the sensitivity side was not.
findings.impact: A matter intended to be privileged or sealed but carrying a label that does not match the table exactly, through a casing difference, a typo, or the same pre-2024 import history that models.py:37-39 documents for the clearance column, becomes readable and writable by any principal of standard clearance in the firm, and the sealed-plus-is_staff brake at policy.py:51-52 never engages because that branch tests the literal string 'sealed'. The failure is silent: nothing logs an unrecognised label. Note the asymmetry, which is what makes this its own finding: on the clearance axis an unknown value maximises the caller's rank, and on the sensitivity axis it minimises the object's protection, so the two defaults fail open in opposite directions and a single fix to one does not address the other.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed on this axis too: default an unrecognised sensitivity to the highest rank rather than to 'standard', or raise PolicyError and log the label. Constrain the column with a CHECK or enum plus a data migration mapping legacy labels, so an unmapped value cannot exist rather than being silently treated as ordinary.

triage.reason: These two lines are the only place sensitivity is compared anywhere in the component, so no other layer re-derives the object's protection level.
case.sensitivity is a stored column with no allowlist on write (models.py:50) and the same import provenance the code documents for the sibling clearance column.
There is no reading in which the default is benign: 20 is exactly the rank of 'standard', so an unknown label is indistinguishable from an ordinary matter rather than being treated cautiously.
The fallback is reached by every read and write decision in the component, since can_read and can_write are the only gates and both use it.

scope.established_by: Grepped every use of SENSITIVITY_RANK and CLEARANCE_RANK in the package and compared the two fallback constants against their respective tables, then checked the column definition for a constraint.
scope.narrowed_by: The write path retains one brake for the literal 'sealed' at policy.py:51-52, but that test is on the exact string, so a mislabelled sealed matter does not benefit from it; the read path has no brake at all.

searched.for: a constraint, enum or validator restricting Case.sensitivity to the four known labels
searched.found: a bare String(32) with default 'standard' and no constraint of any kind

searched.for: a CHECK constraint or a backfill normalising sensitivity values
searched.found: nothing: the migration adds three columns to case_notes, two indexes and two seed rows, and never touches cases.sensitivity

searched.for: whether the field-level projection uses the same fallback, which would widen the finding to what columns are returned
searched.found: visible_fields keys off the principal's clearance against SENSITIVITY_RANK['privileged'], a direct dict index on a literal, so it does not consume the object's sensitivity and is unaffected
